sentences.text: This creature measured roughly 1.2 meters in length, stood 26 centimeters tall, and had a mass of about one kilogram.
Its head featured an elongated shape with stretched-out eye sockets.
The animal walked on two legs, possessing long hind limbs, short forelimbs, hands equipped with large claws, a slender snout filled with numerous tiny teeth, and a rigid tail.
The species appears in Michael Crichton's novels Jurassic Park and The Lost World as a genetically recreated animal called a compy.
In these stories, the creature is shown as a scavenger and coprophage that cleans up the droppings of giant sauropods.
During the second film adaptation, a character named Robert Burke refers to them by the specific name Compsognathus triassicus.
Albert Burrer found the holotype specimen in the spring of 1909 within sediments from the Norian stage of the Triassic period.
The remains were located in the Keuper Formation, specifically the Stubensandstein layer at Pfaffenhoffen, which is now part of Heilbron in Württemberg, Germany.
These remains, cataloged as SMNS 12591, were first described by Fraas in 1912 under the name Hallopus celerrimus before being renamed Procompsognathus triassicus in 1913.

Although the skull was very broken, it indicated a long narrow snout, a large anteorbital fossa, a large orbit, thin jaws with recurved teeth, a large infratemporal fenestra, and a narrower elliptical supratemporal fenestra.
The tibia was approximately 20 percent longer than the femur, a trait linked to cursorial habits that suggests it was a capable runner.
It likely consumed insects, lizards, and other small prey.
Procompsognathus has typically been viewed as a theropod dinosaur, although some researchers have suggested other classifications.
The genus is placed within the family Coelophysidae.
Fraas originally assigned it to the group Dinosauria.
While historically listed as a theropod, some experts now consider Procompsognathus not a dinosaur but a primitive ornithodiran.
The animal lived during the late Triassic Period, roughly 218 to 211 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
Its existence spanned the Norian stage, occurring between 215.38 and 211.18 million years ago.
It is debated whether the holotype skull belongs to a theropod or a crocodylomorph, with Sankar Chatterjee arguing in 1993 that it is a theropod similar to Megapnosaurus.
John Ostrom claimed in 1982 that specimens SMNS 12352 and SMNS 12352a belong to a taxon different from the holotype Procompsognathus.
Fabien Knoll concluded in 2006 and 2008 that specimens SMNS 12352 and SMNS 12352a represent crocodylomorphs or other basal archosaurs, not Procompsognathus.
In 1982, John Ostrom stated that SMNS 12352 and SMNS 12352a originated from a taxon distinct from the holotype.
In 2012, Knoll, following a computed tomography scan, reaffirmed that SMNS 12352 was a crocodylomorph but established that it was different from Saltoposuchus.
